metaDescription: Five Maono podcast and streaming mixers compared: AME2, E2 Gen2, the 3.5mm bundle mixer, G1 Neo and G3, covering preamps, pads, loopback and phantom power.
expertTake: The AME2 is the best overall for a podcaster who wants phantom power, many sound pads and Bluetooth in one console. The E2 Gen2 is the value pick for a two-host show with dual XLR inputs. Anyone recording a single USB voice should skip the mixer and buy a plain USB microphone.
introParagraphs: Compact USB mixers have become the first step up for new podcasters and streamers, giving them faders, effects pads and phantom power without a rack of equipment. The category ranges from simple one-microphone boards to desk consoles with a dozen controls.

What separates them is the number of real microphone inputs, how loopback and Bluetooth are handled, and whether the layout was built for talk shows or for gaming. Settle those three questions before you compare sound effects and lighting.

products.name: Maono AME2 10-channel podcast studio console
products.description:
The AME2 is a ten-channel podcast console that puts a microphone preamp, phantom power, Bluetooth and a bank of eleven customizable sound pads on one panel. Three of the pads can record up to 60 seconds of audio, which turns a jingle or a recorded stinger into a one-press trigger without any software. The built-in preamps support phantom power for condenser XLR microphones, and the high headroom also suits a guitar or bass line input.

Its limitation is the single dedicated microphone path, so it is best for a host who also plays music or takes a guest on a second source. Compared with the E2 Gen2, it has more pads and channels but fewer XLR inputs, and compared with the gaming-oriented G1 Neo, it has a broader layout aimed at talk. For a one-person show with sound effects, it is the most complete option here.

Because there is no firmware to maintain, ownership is easy. Keep the USB cable short, use a pop filter, and write the pad assignments on a label so you remember which key plays which clip. Keep the Bluetooth connection off during recording to avoid stray notification sounds.
products.bestFor: A solo or two-source show with sound pads and condenser or dynamic microphones.
pros: 48V phantom power for condenser XLR microphones
Eleven customizable pads with three that record 60 seconds
Ten channels and Bluetooth for phones and music
High headroom suits a guitar or bass input
cons: Only one dedicated microphone path for a group show
Many pads and knobs invite a longer learning period

products.name: Maono E2 Gen2 dual XLR podcast interface mixer
products.description:
The E2 Gen2 is the two-host answer in this family. It has two premium low-noise preamps on XLR inputs, loopback so computer audio can be mixed back into a stream, Bluetooth for a phone call and eight customizable sound effects on pads. It is sold as a bundle that includes microphones for two people, which makes it an unusually complete starting package.

The tradeoff is scale. With two XLR inputs, it fills a host and guest setup and then stops, while the AME2 offers more channels but only one microphone path. If your show is mostly interview, the E2 Gen2 is better suited, and if your show relies on lots of sound design, the AME2 wins. It is also a compact box, which saves desk space.

In ownership terms, the main worry is the quality of the bundled microphones, which are fine for starting out but may be replaced later. Keep the interface for years and upgrade the microphones when budget allows. Use short balanced cables and keep Bluetooth disconnected while recording. A bundled stand and pop filter in the box make the first session easier, though you may want a boom arm later.
products.bestFor: Two hosts or a host and guest who want XLR microphones and loopback.
pros: Two low-noise XLR preamps for two voices
Loopback keeps computer audio in the mix
Eight customizable sound effects on pads
Bundle includes microphones for a fast start
cons: Only two microphone inputs, so no room to grow

products.name: Maono all-in-one podcast mixer bundle with 3.5mm mic
products.description:
This bundle is the simplest way into the category: an all-in-one audio mixing station with a 3.5mm microphone included. It supports up to two people, four devices and four platforms at once, so a phone, a computer and a console can feed the same stream. Eight built-in effects and four user-recordable slots add variety without extra gear.

The tradeoff is audio quality and growth. The 3.5mm microphone path does not offer phantom power or the preamp headroom of an XLR input, so it will not do justice to a studio dynamic microphone. Compared with the AME2 and E2 Gen2, it is the lowest tier of the group, and it is meant for someone who wants to start streaming quickly rather than build a long-term studio.

Ownership is minimal because there is little to break, but expect to replace the microphone first. Keep the cables tidy, and note that all four devices share one mix, so a quiet phone call and a loud game may need level changes. Treat it as a stepping stone.
products.bestFor: A beginner streamer who wants one box for phone, PC and console.
pros: Handles four devices and four platforms at once
Eight built-in effects plus four user recordable slots
Included 3.5mm microphone for a quick start
Lowest tier of the Maono mixers here
cons: No XLR input for studio microphones

products.name: Maono G1 Neo gaming mixer with XLR and 48V
products.description:
The G1 Neo is the gaming-oriented model, with RGB lighting, four custom soundpads and a voice change feature. A built-in preamp and 48V phantom power let it drive a condenser XLR microphone properly, and Bluetooth takes a phone call. It is a compact box aimed at streamers who want effects they can trigger live without opening a program.

Its tradeoff is that it is designed for fun rather than for the dull realities of long interviews. With one XLR input, it matches the AME2 in microphone count but has fewer pads and less channel flexibility. Compared with the G3 below, it is simpler, cheaper to learn, and has fewer routing options for a streamer who needs submixes.

Ownership is easy. The lighting is a feature rather than a durability concern, and the knobs are small, so be gentle. Choose a decent XLR cable, add a pop filter and set the gain once. The voice change effect is fun for a segment but best left off for normal recording. Keep the lighting on a low setting if the glow distracts on camera.
products.bestFor: A gamer or new streamer who wants lighting, pads and an XLR input.
pros: XLR input with 48V phantom for condenser microphones
Four custom soundpads for live effects
Voice change feature adds fun segments
Bluetooth takes a phone call into the mix
cons: Gaming-oriented features are wasted on a pure talk show

products.name: Maono G3 4-fader gaming mixer with 3 submixes
products.description:
The G3 is a desktop mixer built for Windows PC streamers, and its defining feature is flexible mapping. Any audio source can be assigned to one of four faders, and three submixes let you build separate audio experiences for yourself, your viewers and a recording. Dual PC support makes it suitable for streamers who run a gaming machine and a capture machine.

The cost of that flexibility is a setup process. Mapping sources and submixes takes thought, and a podcaster who just needs two microphones is paying for routing they will not use. Compared with the G1 Neo, it is a more serious streaming tool, and compared with the AME2, it replaces pads with faders and submixes.

Ownership favors people who like to tune. Save a mapping that matches your streaming layout, keep the software updated, and note that the platform support is Windows-focused. Keep the cabling stable between the two PCs, and test your layout before going live.
products.bestFor: A Windows PC streamer who needs separate submixes and fast fader control.
pros: Maps any audio source to four faders
Three submixes for separate listeners
Supports dual PC streaming setups
XLR interface for a studio microphone
cons: Setup takes more thought than a simple podcast board

buyingCriteria.explanation: The E2 Gen2 offers two XLR preamps, while the AME2 and G1 Neo offer a single XLR path and the bundle relies on a 3.5mm microphone. Count how many people will talk at once, and choose the mixer with that many real preamps. Total channel count, such as the AME2's ten, includes non-microphone sources. A fair rule is one real preamp per regular voice plus one spare, because a spare input saves you when a guest brings a second microphone.

Condenser microphones need 48V from the XLR input, which the AME2, G1 Neo and E2 Gen2 supply. The 3.5mm bundle cannot power a condenser at all. If you plan to use a studio condenser, make sure the mixer has phantom power on the input you intend to use. If you are unsure whether a microphone needs phantom power, check its specification sheet before connecting, since only condensers require it.

Loopback lets you mix computer audio back into a stream without feedback. The E2 Gen2 offers it, and the G3 adds three submixes and dual PC support. A talk show with remote guests benefits from loopback, while a plain recording benefits little. Remote guests are the other reason to value loopback, since a call on a computer can be mixed in without a second device.

The AME2 has eleven pads and the E2 Gen2 has eight effects, while the G3 swaps pads for four mappable faders. Pads suit a show with lots of stingers, and faders suit a streamer who rides levels. Choose by how you actually work. Remember that pad clips need to be loaded in advance and labelled, or the board turns into guesswork on air.

The G3 is designed around Windows PCs, while the AME2 and E2 Gen2 are more general interfaces. Check the operating system you use and whether the mixer needs software for full control. A mismatch is a common return reason. Install any companion software on a spare day, not minutes before a stream, because driver prompts can cost time.

The E2 Gen2 bundle includes microphones and the 3.5mm bundle includes a 3.5mm microphone. Bundled microphones help you start, but they are rarely the best you can buy. Budget for an upgrade after a few months if audio quality matters. A good dynamic microphone and a boom arm usually improve a recording more than any mixer upgrade does.

specDecoder.meaning: A voltage sent down the XLR cable to power condenser microphones. Dynamic microphones do not need it. Turn it off when switching to a dynamic microphone to be safe.
specDecoder.watchFor: The AME2, G1 Neo and E2 Gen2 supply it, and the 3.5mm bundle does not.

specDecoder.meaning: A route that sends computer audio back into the mix so a stream hears it. It avoids feedback by design.
specDecoder.watchFor: The E2 Gen2 lists loopback, and the G3 offers submixes for similar control.

specDecoder.meaning: A separate mix for a defined listener, such as you, your viewers or a recording. It lets each get a different balance. Think of each submix as a separate pair of headphones with its own balance.
specDecoder.watchFor: The G3 has three submixes, which others in the group do not.

specDecoder.meaning: A button that plays a stored sound or effect. Some pads can record a clip of a set length. Short clips of two to five seconds work best for live use.
specDecoder.watchFor: The AME2 has eleven and three record up to 60 seconds.

specDecoder.meaning: A small jack used for consumer headsets and lavalier microphones. It lacks the balanced signal and gain of XLR. Adapters can bridge the gap, but they do not add gain or balance.
specDecoder.watchFor: The bundle mixer uses 3.5mm, so it will not suit a studio dynamic microphone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Microphone design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared XLR inputs, phantom power and the use of 3.5mm jacks. The E2 Gen2 has two XLR preamps and the bundle relies on 3.5mm. Real microphone paths decided the first scores. We also noted whether the preamp can drive a quiet dynamic microphone without noise.

howWeEvaluated.title: Routing and mixes
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at loopback, submixes and dual PC support. The G3 provides three submixes and the E2 Gen2 provides loopback. Routing flexibility mattered for streamers. We counted how many outputs each unit offers for monitors and recorders.

howWeEvaluated.title: Effects and pads
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pad counts and recording features. The AME2 has eleven pads, three of which record 60 seconds. Useful pads raised the score for effect-heavy shows. We noted which pads can be recorded directly on the unit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which operating systems and device types each model supports. The G3 targets Windows PC and the bundle supports four devices. Broad compatibility scored higher. We also checked that each unit works with common streaming software.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered the likely lifetime of knobs, jacks and bundled microphones. Owner feedback patterns on small controls informed the scores. Simpler layouts scored higher for beginners. We noted how clearly each board labels its controls.

cards.label: Pad-based consoles
cards.text: The AME2 and E2 Gen2 use pads for stingers and effects. They suit talk shows and comedy segments with frequent clips.

cards.label: Fader-based mixers
cards.text: The G3 maps sources to four faders and offers three submixes. It suits streamers who need constant level control.

howToChoose.note: Talk shows should pick pads, and PC streamers should pick faders.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for XLR inputs with phantom power, a clean headphone output and loopback for remote guests. Extra effects matter less than a quiet preamp. Make sure the mixer matches your computer.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The E2 Gen2 is the best fit for two hosts, while the AME2 suits a solo show with many sound clips. The gaming models fit hybrid streaming and podcasting.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you run dual PCs, need submixes or want a rich pad bank. The G3 and AME2 provide that headroom.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you are starting out with one headset or a single microphone. The 3.5mm bundle and G1 Neo cover that need at the lowest tiers.

maintenance.why: A failing cable causes crackle that mimics a bad preamp. Swap cables before blaming the mixer. Coil cables loosely so the internal wires do not break.
Dust builds up in small controls and causes scratchy movement. A dry brush is usually enough. A cotton swab dipped in contact cleaner works for small knobs.
Software updates keep routing and pad functions compatible with your operating system. Update between shows. Read the release notes first so a change does not surprise you.
A label avoids hitting the wrong effect on air. It also helps a guest host run the board. A strip of tape under each pad is enough.
A simple cover keeps dust and liquids away from the controls. It costs little and extends life.

faq.q: Which Maono mixer is best for podcasting?
faq.a: The AME2 is the most complete podcast console, and the E2 Gen2 suits two hosts. The G-series are aimed at streamers. If you only record one voice and add sound effects later in editing, the pads are less important than the preamp.

faq.q: Do I need a mixer or a USB microphone?
faq.a: A single USB microphone is simpler for a solo host. A mixer is worth it when you want pads, loopback or two XLR microphones. Pairing a mixer with a USB microphone is rarely needed, so decide on one path early.

faq.q: Will these work with condenser microphones?
faq.a: The AME2, E2 Gen2 and G1 Neo supply 48V phantom power. The 3.5mm bundle does not power a condenser. If you are unsure, check the product page for the words phantom power next to the input.

faq.q: How many people can record at once?
faq.a: The E2 Gen2 supports two XLR microphones. The AME2 and G1 Neo support one XLR microphone plus other sources. Plan for a short test recording of ten minutes before every show, since problems appear quickly.

faq.q: How long will these mixers last?
faq.a: They are lightly built, so the wear items are knobs, jacks and cables. Handle them gently and they can serve for years. Keep the unit away from heat and spills, and avoid pulling on cables.

Bluetooth works for a phone call or music, but quality is lower than USB or analog. Use it for convenience, not for the best sound. For important interviews, ask the guest to use a wired connection instead.
